name: Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride
description: Master the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride in BJJ. Learn gi-based blood choke mechanics using dynamic turtle control and circular walking pressure to finish.
overview:
The Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride is a gi-based blood choke that capitalizes on the dynamic control mechanics unique to the Rodeo Ride position on a turtled opponent. Unlike the standard Clock Choke from static turtle top, the Rodeo Ride variant leverages the asymmetric hip pressure and near-arm control already established in the ride to feed a deep cross-collar grip before the opponent can address the choking threat. The attacker's perpendicular angle and loaded hip position create a natural launching point for the circular walk that generates finishing pressure.

What makes this variation particularly dangerous is that the Rodeo Ride's constant pressure cycling disguises the choke entry. The opponent is already defending multiple back attack and submission threats, so the lapel feed can be inserted during a transition between other attacks. Once the cross-collar grip is secured, the attacker walks their hips around the opponent's head in an arc while sprawling weight through their chest, compressing both carotid arteries using the lapel as a fulcrum against the opponent's neck. The Rodeo Ride's established hip control prevents the primary escape of sitting back to guard, which is the most common defense against standard Clock Chokes.

This submission is most effective when chained with other Rodeo Ride attacks—threatening the back take forces the opponent to defend their hips, which opens the collar for the choke entry. The technique requires precise timing between releasing near-arm control to feed the lapel and maintaining enough positional pressure to prevent escape during the grip transition.

injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for serious injury if held after unconsciousness

Remove your weight from opponent's back and create space

attacker.name: Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride. Step-by-step lapel feed, walking arc mechanics, and finishing pressure from dynamic turtle control.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride requires integrating the dynamic pressure management of the ride with precise gi grip work. The key advantage over a standard turtle-top Clock Choke is that Rodeo Ride's established hip loading and near-arm control create a two-stage entry: first you threaten back attacks to occupy the opponent's defensive attention, then exploit the opening to feed the cross-collar grip. Your perpendicular angle means the walking arc to finish the choke is shorter, and your hip pressure prevents the sit-back escape that defeats most Clock Choke attempts from conventional turtle top. The technique rewards practitioners who can maintain ride pressure while executing fine motor grip work under resistance.
key_principles: Disguise the lapel feed within your normal Rodeo Ride attack cycling—never telegraph the choke entry
Maintain hip pressure throughout the grip transition to prevent the opponent from sitting back to guard
Walk your hips in a tight arc around the opponent's head rather than pulling the lapel—let body weight create the choking pressure
Keep your chest connected to the opponent's back during the entire finishing sequence to prevent space creation
Control the near arm until the cross-collar grip is deep enough that releasing it won't compromise the choke
Sprawl your legs behind you as you walk around to maximize downward pressure through the choking grip
setup_requirements: Established Rodeo Ride control with hip pressure loaded on opponent's back and near-arm controlled
Opponent in defensive turtle with knees under hips—not flattened, which would indicate mount transition instead
Access to opponent's far-side lapel or collar for the cross-collar grip feed
Posted leg base stable enough to begin walking arc without losing balance during grip transition
Opponent defending back take threats, creating the window to feed the collar grip

execution_steps.action: Threaten back take to occupy defenses
execution_steps.description: From established Rodeo Ride, initiate a back take attempt by threatening to insert hooks or establish seat belt control. This forces the opponent to commit their defensive attention to preventing back exposure, creating the opening to feed the collar grip. Your hip pressure should be heavy on their back with chest connected to their shoulder area.

As the opponent defends the back take, release your far-side hand and reach across to feed your hand deep into their far-side lapel at collar level. The grip should be palm-down with four fingers inside the collar, knuckles pressing against the side of their neck. Feed the grip as deep as possible—shallow grips require more walking distance to finish and give the opponent more time to defend.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds, executed during opponent's defensive reaction

execution_steps.description: With your other hand, grip the near-side collar or the back of the gi at belt level. This secondary grip serves as the anchor point that prevents the opponent from pulling away as you begin walking. The near-side grip also controls the opponent's ability to turn into you and maintains the rotational tension needed for the choke. Keep your elbow tight to their body.

Start walking your hips in a tight arc toward the opponent's head, maintaining chest-to-back contact throughout. Move perpendicular to their spine initially, then continue walking past their head. Each step should sprawl your weight progressively lower, driving your hip pressure through the choking grip and into their neck. Keep your knees off the mat and walk on your toes to maximize pressure transfer.

As you pass the opponent's head, sprawl your hips to the mat and drive your weight forward through your chest and into the grip. Your body should be nearly perpendicular to the opponent at this point, with your hips on the far side of their head. The sprawl creates the downward force that compresses the lapel against both carotid arteries. Pull your choking elbow toward your own hip to tighten the noose.
execution_steps.timing: 2-3 seconds to fully settle the sprawl

execution_steps.description: Complete the choke by continuing to walk your feet away from the opponent while pulling your choking grip toward your hip and driving your shoulder into their upper back. The combination of your body weight sprawled over them and the lapel tension across their neck creates bilateral carotid compression. Apply pressure progressively, giving your training partner time to recognize the choke and tap. Do not jerk or explosively tighten.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin and drives forward to create space before grip is deep
common_counters.your_response: Maintain hip pressure and wait—re-threaten the back take to force them to open the chin, then re-feed the grip. Do not chase the collar with the chin tucked, as you will lose riding position.

common_counters.counter: Opponent sits back to half guard or closed guard during grip transition
common_counters.your_response: If you still have the collar grip, maintain it and transition to a guillotine or front headlock attack as they sit through. If the grip is lost, accept the guard position and work your top game.

common_counters.counter: Opponent rolls toward the choking side to relieve pressure
common_counters.your_response: Follow the roll and take the back as they expose it. Their roll actually assists your transition to back control with the collar grip already established, which sets up a Bow and Arrow Choke.

common_counters.counter: Opponent posts far arm and attempts to stand during the walking arc
common_counters.your_response: Accelerate your walking arc and sprawl immediately to collapse their posting arm with your body weight. If they achieve standing, transition to a standing clock choke variation by hanging your weight from the collar grip.

common_errors.error: Releasing hip pressure to reach for the collar grip, creating space for escape
common_errors.consequence: Opponent sits back to guard or stands up before the choke can be established, losing the Rodeo Ride position entirely
common_errors.correction: Maintain hip-to-back contact throughout the grip feed. Use the back take threat to create the opening rather than lifting off to reach the collar.

common_errors.error: Feeding a shallow collar grip that doesn't reach past the centerline of the neck
common_errors.consequence: The choke becomes an airway choke rather than a blood choke, requiring excessive force and giving the opponent time to defend
common_errors.correction: Feed the grip as deep as possible—four fingers should reach past the opponent's far-side carotid. A deep initial grip means less walking distance is needed to finish.

common_errors.error: Pulling the lapel with arms instead of driving pressure through body weight and walking
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly and the choke lacks sufficient pressure to finish against a defended neck. Opponent can outlast the arm-based squeeze.
common_errors.correction: Keep the choking arm locked in position and generate all finishing pressure through your walking arc and hip sprawl. The body moves, the grip stays fixed.

common_errors.error: Walking arc too wide, losing chest-to-back connection during the finish
common_errors.consequence: Gap between your chest and their back allows opponent to flatten, turn, or create frames that prevent the choke from tightening
common_errors.correction: Walk in a tight arc with your chest glued to their upper back and shoulder. Your body should rotate around the grip point, not drift away from it.

common_errors.error: Attempting the choke when opponent's turtle is already compromised and flattening
common_errors.consequence: A flattened opponent is better attacked with mount transitions or crucifix rather than Clock Choke, which requires an upright turtle base to function
common_errors.correction: Read the opponent's posture—if they are flattening, transition to mount or crucifix. Save the Clock Choke for opponents maintaining a strong turtle base.

common_errors.error: Telegraphing the choke by immediately reaching for the collar without first threatening other attacks
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the Clock Choke setup early and tucks chin, fights grips, or sits back before you can establish the collar grip
common_errors.correction: Always set up the choke within your normal Rodeo Ride attack cycle. Threaten the back take or crucifix first, then feed the collar when their defensive attention is elsewhere.

training_progressions.description: Partner holds static turtle. Practice feeding the cross-collar grip from Rodeo Ride repeatedly, focusing on getting four fingers past the far-side carotid. No resistance. Build the motor pattern of maintaining hip pressure while executing the grip feed. 20 repetitions per side.

With the grip already established, practice the walking arc around the opponent's head. Focus on staying on toes, sprawling progressively, and maintaining chest connection. Partner provides light defensive frames. Work on generating pressure through body positioning rather than arm strength.

training_progressions.focus: Chaining from Rodeo Ride attacks to choke entry
training_progressions.description: Practice the full sequence: establish Rodeo Ride, threaten back take, feed collar during defensive reaction, execute walking finish. Partner provides moderate resistance and attempts basic defenses (chin tuck, grip fighting). Focus on timing the grip feed during the opponent's defensive transitions.

Positional sparring starting from Rodeo Ride. Top practitioner attempts Clock Choke within their normal attack cycling. Bottom practitioner defends fully. Work on reading when the Clock Choke is available versus when to pursue other attacks. Develop sensitivity for grip depth and finishing pressure under resistance.

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures does the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride primarily target?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Clock Choke targets both carotid arteries simultaneously using the opponent's own gi lapel as the compression mechanism. The cross-collar grip positions the lapel across the front and sides of the neck, and as the attacker walks around and sprawls, the lapel presses against the left and right carotid arteries, restricting blood flow to the brain. This bilateral compression causes unconsciousness within 8-12 seconds if the choke is fully locked. The technique is a blood choke, not an airway choke, which is why a deep collar grip past the centerline is essential.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why does the Rodeo Ride position create a superior Clock Choke entry compared to standard turtle top?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Rodeo Ride provides three advantages over standard turtle top for Clock Choke entry. First, the established hip pressure and near-arm control mean the opponent is already defending multiple threats, disguising the collar grip feed. Second, the perpendicular angle of Rodeo Ride shortens the walking arc needed to finish, since you are already partially around the opponent's body. Third, the dynamic pressure cycling of Rodeo Ride prevents the sit-back escape that defeats most Clock Choke attempts from conventional turtle top positions, because your hips are actively loaded on their back.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent starts tucking their chin aggressively when they feel the collar grip being fed—what adjustment prevents escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Do not force the grip past a tucked chin, as this telegraphs the choke and wastes energy. Instead, maintain the partial grip and re-threaten a back take by shifting your hips toward inserting hooks. When the opponent redirects their defensive attention from chin protection to hip defense, the chin naturally opens and you can deepen the collar grip. Alternatively, use your near-side hand to cross-face and rotate their head slightly, creating the space needed to feed the grip deeper. The key principle is creating a dilemma where defending the chin opens the back, and defending the back opens the chin.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key indicators that the choke is properly locked and approaching the breaking point?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The choke is properly locked when you feel bilateral tension across both sides of the opponent's neck through the lapel, your chest is firmly connected to their upper back with no gap, and your hip weight is driving through the grip into their neck. The opponent's face will typically flush red and their breathing will become labored. Their defensive movements will become increasingly urgent and less coordinated. You should feel the lapel tightening against their neck without needing to squeeze with your arms—the pressure is generated by your body weight and position. If you are muscling the grip, the choke is not properly set.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the proper release protocol when your training partner taps to the Clock Choke?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately release the cross-collar grip upon any tap signal—verbal, hand tap, or foot tap. Remove your chest pressure and hip weight from the opponent's back and create space by moving away. Do not maintain any grip or body contact after the tap. Allow your partner to recover in a neutral position without any residual pressure. Check on their condition before resuming training. If the opponent went unconscious, place them in recovery position, monitor breathing, and seek medical attention. Never re-apply pressure after a tap to demonstrate the choke was locked.

knowledge_assessment.question: What grip adjustments should you make during the walking arc if you feel the choke loosening?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the choke loosens during the walking arc, first check that your chest has not separated from the opponent's back—re-establish chest contact immediately. Then pull your choking elbow tighter toward your own hip to take slack out of the lapel. If the grip has slipped shallow, you may need to pause the walk, re-sprawl your weight to pin the opponent, and re-feed the grip deeper before continuing. Avoid the temptation to walk faster to compensate—speed without depth creates an airway choke that is uncomfortable but won't finish. A brief pause to reset the grip is better than completing a loose arc.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you abandon the Clock Choke attempt and transition to a different attack from Rodeo Ride?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Abandon the Clock Choke when the opponent successfully strips the collar grip before you begin the walking arc, when they sit back past the point where your hip pressure can prevent guard recovery, or when they flatten completely to the mat. If the grip is stripped, immediately re-establish Rodeo Ride control and cycle to a different attack—the back take or crucifix. If they sit back, transition to a front headlock or guillotine if the collar grip is still held. If they flatten, advance to mount. Never chase a lost Clock Choke by repeatedly reaching for the collar, as this compromises your riding position.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you manage the choke application speed to ensure training partner safety?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Apply the finishing pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum, never explosively. The walking arc itself should be deliberate and controlled. As you feel the choke tightening, maintain steady pressure rather than jerking or pulsing the grip. Monitor your partner's response throughout—if they are not tapping but showing signs of distress such as panicked movement, slowing movements, or going limp, release immediately. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness within seconds of full application, so the controlled approach gives your partner adequate time to recognize the threat and tap before consciousness is affected.

knowledge_assessment.question: What common finishing error causes the Clock Choke to become an uncomfortable but non-finishing airway choke?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most common cause of an airway-only choke is a shallow collar grip that does not reach past the centerline of the opponent's neck. When the grip is shallow, the lapel presses against the trachea and front of the throat rather than compressing the carotid arteries on both sides. This creates pain and discomfort but will not cause a blood-choke finish. The correction is to ensure four fingers are fed deep past the far-side carotid before beginning the walk. A properly deep grip positioned at collar level, not throat level, naturally targets the lateral neck structures.

knowledge_assessment.question: In competition, what strategic advantages does attacking the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride offer over taking the back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride offers a direct submission path without needing to secure hooks for back control points, which can be time-consuming against a well-defended turtle. In points-based competition, the Clock Choke can finish the match immediately from a position where no points have been scored yet—you bypass the incremental point-scoring of back take and go straight to submission. Additionally, opponents who are highly skilled at defending back takes often leave the neck more vulnerable because their defensive priorities focus on hook prevention and hip defense. The Clock Choke exploits this defensive allocation.

defender.name: Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride Defender
defender.description: Defend the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride in BJJ. Recognition cues, grip stripping techniques, escape paths, and guard recovery from turtle under choke threat.
defender.overview:
Defending the Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride requires addressing two simultaneous problems: the Rodeo Ride control that limits your mobility and the lapel grip that threatens the choke. The challenge is compounded because the attacker uses their normal Rodeo Ride attack cycling to disguise the choke entry, meaning you may not recognize the threat until the collar grip is already partially established. Effective defense begins with recognizing the grip feed early—before the attacker reaches the far-side lapel—and prioritizing grip stripping over positional escape. Once the collar grip is deep and the attacker begins walking, defensive options narrow significantly.

The defender's primary strategic objective is to prevent the collar grip from being established in the first place by keeping elbows tight and chin protected while working standard turtle escape sequences. If the grip is established, the defense shifts to stripping it before the walking arc begins. If the walk has started, the final defensive option is to sit back aggressively to closed or half guard, accepting the guard position rather than allowing the choke to finish. Understanding this defensive timeline—prevent the grip, strip the grip, escape the position—gives the defender a framework for making decisions under pressure.
key_principles: Protect the collar area by keeping chin tucked and elbows tight to prevent the initial lapel feed
Recognize the choke setup early by feeling for the hand reaching across to the far-side collar
Strip the collar grip immediately before the attacker can begin the walking arc—grip stripping is time-critical
If the grip cannot be stripped, sit back aggressively to guard rather than remaining in turtle under choke threat
Fight the near-side collar control as well as the cross-collar grip, as both are needed for the choke to finish
Never expose the neck by turning your head away from the choking side, which deepens the grip path
recognition_cues: Attacker's far-side hand releases near-arm control or back attack grip and reaches toward your collar area
Feeling fingers sliding inside your far-side lapel or collar, particularly with a palm-down orientation
Attacker shifts weight slightly to the side to create reach for the collar grip feed
Change in attacker's pressure pattern from back-take threatening to settling weight more centrally on your back
Attacker's near-side hand moves to your belt line or near-side collar, indicating secondary grip establishment

defensive_options.action: Strip the collar grip with both hands before the walking arc begins
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon feeling fingers entering the collar—this is the highest-percentage defense and must be executed within the first 2-3 seconds of grip establishment
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker returns to standard Rodeo Ride without choke threat, must re-attempt setup
defensive_options.risk: Releasing your turtle defensive posture to strip grips temporarily exposes you to back take or crucifix

defensive_options.action: Aggressive sit-back to closed guard or half guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the collar grip is established and the attacker begins the walking arc—sitting back removes the opponent's ability to sprawl and walk, collapsing the choke mechanics
defensive_options.if_successful: Transition to guard position where the Clock Choke cannot be finished, though opponent may retain collar grip for other attacks
defensive_options.risk: Sitting back against a well-timed choke may accelerate the finish if the grip is already deep enough

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker and establish defensive frames
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the collar grip is shallow and the attacker has not yet committed to the walking arc—turning in prevents the perpendicular angle needed for the choke
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the choke angle and may lead to guard recovery or scramble
defensive_options.risk: Turning in can expose the back if the opponent redirects to a back take instead of pursuing the choke

defensive_options.action: Explosive stand-up while stripping collar grip
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker's base is compromised during the grip transition—requires timing the moment when their posted leg shifts for the walking arc
defensive_options.if_successful: Escape to standing position, resetting the engagement entirely
defensive_options.risk: If the collar grip is maintained during stand-up, the attacker can transition to a standing choke variation

escape_paths: Sit-back to closed guard by dropping hips to the mat and threading legs between you and the attacker, collapsing the turtle structure that the choke requires
Granby roll away from the choking side to invert and face the opponent, disrupting the walking arc angle and creating guard recovery opportunity
Explosive technical stand-up by posting the far-side hand, stripping the collar grip, and driving to standing position while the attacker's base is transitioning

favorable_outcomes.how: Sit back aggressively when you feel the collar grip being established, threading your legs into guard before the attacker can complete the walking arc. Accept the guard position as a significant improvement over being choked in turtle.

Strip the collar grip within the first 2-3 seconds using both hands, then immediately re-establish defensive turtle posture. The attacker returns to standard Rodeo Ride position without the choking threat, buying time for other escape attempts.

common_errors.error: Failing to recognize the choke setup until the walking arc has already begun
common_errors.consequence: Defensive options are severely limited once the attacker is walking—the choke tightens with each step and grip stripping becomes nearly impossible under sprawl pressure
common_errors.correction: Train sensitivity to feel the collar grip being fed. The moment you feel fingers entering the collar, react immediately—even a 2-second delay can be the difference between an easy grip strip and a locked choke.

common_errors.error: Turning the head away from the choking side to avoid the grip
common_errors.consequence: Turning the head away actually opens the far-side collar and deepens the grip path, making the choke easier to establish and finish
common_errors.correction: Turn your chin toward the choking side to close the collar space. Tuck your chin to your chest and turn slightly toward the attacker's grip hand to compress the available space for the lapel feed.

common_errors.error: Staying in turtle and attempting to defend the choke through chin tuck alone without escaping
common_errors.consequence: A persistent attacker will eventually pry open the chin tuck through pressure cycling, and passive defense only delays the submission rather than preventing it
common_errors.correction: Use the chin tuck as a temporary measure while executing an active escape—sit back to guard, granby roll, or strip the grip. The chin tuck buys time, but time must be used for escape, not just survival.

common_errors.error: Reaching behind to strip the collar grip with one hand while maintaining turtle base with the other
common_errors.consequence: One-handed grip strips are rarely successful against a deep collar grip, and the reaching arm can be captured for crucifix or armbar attacks
common_errors.correction: Commit both hands to the grip strip—use one hand to control the attacker's wrist and the other to peel fingers from the collar. Accept that your turtle base will be briefly compromised during the strip.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the earliest recognition cue that a Clock Choke is being set up from Rodeo Ride?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The earliest cue is feeling the attacker's far-side hand release its current grip—whether that was near-arm control, back attack grip, or belt grip—and move toward your collar area. This grip transition represents the moment of maximum vulnerability for the attacker because they are giving up established control to pursue the choke. Recognizing this transition is the defender's best opportunity, because reacting at this point allows you to strip a shallow grip rather than fighting a deep one.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you tap to a Clock Choke to prevent injury?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap as soon as you feel bilateral pressure on both sides of your neck and cannot execute an escape. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness within 8-12 seconds of full application, and there is no benefit to waiting until the last moment. If the collar grip is deep, the walking arc is past your head, and the attacker is sprawled with weight through the grip, the choke is structurally complete. Tap clearly using hand taps, foot taps, or verbal submission. If your hands are trapped, use foot taps or verbal signals immediately. Never try to tough out a locked blood choke.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is sitting back to guard preferable to remaining in turtle once the collar grip is deep?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Clock Choke mechanically requires the opponent to be in an elevated turtle position so the attacker can walk around the head and sprawl. When you sit back to guard, you collapse the structure the choke depends on—the attacker cannot walk around your head if you are facing them in guard. While sitting back concedes the guard position, this is a significant improvement over being submitted. The attacker may retain the collar grip in guard, but they cannot finish the Clock Choke from inside your guard. You trade a submission threat for a positional disadvantage, which is always the correct exchange.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive options remain once the attacker has fully committed to the walking arc?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Once the walk has begun, your primary option is an aggressive sit-back to guard before the sprawl completes. Drop your hips to the mat and thread your legs in front of the attacker as they walk past your head. Secondary option is a granby roll away from the choking direction, using the roll to invert and face the attacker, which disrupts the arc angle. Grip stripping during the active walk is very difficult because the attacker's body weight is driving through the grip. The key is explosive timing—act within the first 1-2 steps of the walk before the sprawl locks the position.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying choke setup cues from Rodeo Ride

Defender calls out which attack is being attempted as soon as they recognize it. No escape attempts yet—focus entirely on reading the attacker's intentions through grip changes and weight shifts. 10 reps of each attack randomized.

training_progressions.focus: Collar grip removal timing and technique
training_progressions.description: Partner feeds the collar grip at various depths while defender practices two-handed grip strips. Start with shallow grips and progressive to deeper grips. Practice the sequence: feel the grip, turn chin toward choking side, control wrist with one hand, peel fingers with the other. Light resistance building to moderate.

Full Rodeo Ride defense rounds where defender must recognize the Clock Choke threat and execute the appropriate escape: grip strip for early detection, sit-back to guard for established grips, granby roll for advanced escapes. Partner provides increasing resistance. Focus on decision-making under pressure.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance Clock Choke defense from Rodeo Ride
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring where attacker is instructed to prioritize Clock Choke from Rodeo Ride. Defender practices the full defensive timeline under competition-level resistance. Debrief after each round to identify the moment where defense succeeded or failed and which recognition cue was present.
